FPGA-Based Dynamically Reconfigurable SQL Query Processing
DANIEL ZIENER, FLORIAN BAUER, ANDREAS BECHER, CHRISTOPHER DENNL,                                                          25
and KLAUS MEYER-WEGENER, Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU)
UTE SCHÜRFELD, IBM Deutschland Research & Development GmbH
JÜRGEN TEICH, Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU)
JÖRG-STEPHAN VOGT and HELMUT WEBER, IBM Deutschland Research
& Development GmbH



In this article, we propose an FPGA-based SQL query processing approach exploiting the capabilities of
partial dynamic reconfiguration of modern FPGAs. After the analysis of an incoming query, a query-specific
hardware processing unit is generated on the fly and loaded on the FPGA for immediate query execution.
For each query, a specialized hardware accelerator pipeline is composed and configured on the FPGA from
a set of presynthesized hardware modules. These partially reconfigurable hardware modules are gathered
in a library covering all major SQL operations like restrictions and aggregations, as well as more complex
operations such as joins and sorts. Moreover, this holistic query processing approach in hardware supports
different data processing strategies including row- as column-wise data processing in order to optimize data
communication and processing. This article gives an overview of the proposed query processing methodology
and the corresponding library of modules. Additionally, a performance analysis is introduced that is able to
estimate the processing time of a query for different processing strategies and different communication and
processing architecture configurations. With the help of this performance analysis, architectural bottlenecks
may be exposed and future optimized architectures, besides the two prototypes presented here, may be
determined.
Categories and Subject Descriptors: B.5.1 [Register-Transfer-Level Implementation]: Design—Data-
path design; C.3 [Special-Purpose and Application-based Systems]: Microprocessor/Microcomputer
Applications; H.2.4 [Database Management]: Systems—Query processing
General Terms: Design, Performance
Additional Key Words and Phrases: FPGA, dynamic partial reconfiguration, SQL processing, reconfigurable
computing

1. INTRODUCTION
One of the big challenges in the IT sector today is the handling of an ever-growing
amount of data. The annual amount of data that is created, captured, or replicated
worldwide increases by a factor of 10 every 5 years [Gantz et al. 2008]. Storing all these
data is one challenge; processing and analyzing them on demand is another one. In
fact, the growth of data even outnumbers Moore’s law of digital-circuit complexity. This
means that it is impossible to handle this amount of data by just using more processing
resources. At the same time, the energy consumption of all data centers worldwide
increases by 16.7% each year [Koomey 2008]. In 2013, the energy consumption of all
IT facilities together approached 10% of the worldwide energy generation [Mills 2013],
and it will increase further. This forces us to investigate more efficient data-processing
approaches.
   The more important kinds of data are stored in relational database management
systems (RDBMSs), which are able to load, analyze, and process the data based on
requested inquiries, mostly given in the form of SQL queries [SQL 2008]. Therefore,
efficient query processing can on the one hand increase the performance of a database
processing system and on the other hand reduce the energy consumption. Hardware
accelerators are able to reach the goal of increasing the efficiency by exploiting natural
parallelism of reconfigurable hardware, as available in FPGAs. Consequently, it is
worthwhile to investigate the use of FPGAs in the field of database applications in
general and for query execution purposes in particular. In analyzing the data stored
in huge tables, which are common in data warehouse applications [Inmon 2002], the
offload of restrictions, joins, and aggregations to an FPGA can increase the efficiency
of query processing substantially.
   However, a static hardware approach is not suitable to cover all operator types used
in these queries. With the help of partial dynamic reconfiguration, however, techniques
for query-specific data-path generation can be used to increase the efficiency of FPGA-
based accelerators. Partially reconfigurable modules stemming from a library of SQL
operators can be composed on the fly to form a query data path and can be loaded onto
the FPGA. Moreover, this library can be extended continuously to offer new operators
or SQL constructs.
   In this article, we give an overview of such a novel FPGA-based partially recon-
figurable query processing system. This system consists of a static hardware part,
including communication and configuration interfaces; a library of partially reconfig-
urable modules, which covers all common SQL operators; and software running on
the host system to analyze an incoming query, select partially reconfigurable modules
from the library, and determine feasible placements for them, as well as controlling the
communication to and configuration of the FPGA. This query processing system has
evolved from a first publication of basic concepts [Dennl et al. 2012] to a mature and
complete design flow for query processing as presented in this article. Starting with
just restrictions [Dennl et al. 2012], aggregations [Dennl et al. 2013], and join and sort
[Becher et al. 2014], the novel hash-join and column-based processing modules, intro-
duced in this article for the first time, complete the portfolio of supported operations.
One of the main challenges was the combination of streaming-based operations with
operations using multiple inputs and buffers for storing intermediate results. In our
proposed system architecture, this is solved by introducing different kinds of partial
reconfigurable areas for SQL operators implemented in a streamed-based manner and
modules using more than one input and/or external memory access. Furthermore, in-
vestigations to process table data column-wise by introducing special modules in order
to reduce the amount of incoming data are analyzed and presented. The main idea is
to use the given static system and only introduce new modules that are able to pro-
cess data column-wise and modules doing row-to-column transformations. Moreover,

  ACM Transactions on Reconfigurable Technology and Systems, Vol. 9, No. 4, Article 25, Publication date: August 2016.
FPGA-Based Dynamically Reconfigurable SQL Query Processing                                                        25:3

a calculus for performance assessment is presented in this article that gives us the
possibility to evaluate the processing time of a query on different, even nonexistent
architectures with different parameters, for example, throughput of communication
interfaces. It also allows us to explore the rich facets of different processing possibili-
ties by combining different modules and different implementations of the same query
operations, for example, processing a join operation as a hash or rather a sort-merge-
join. With the help of this performance calculus, we are able to choose at runtime the
best configuration of our SQL processing system for a given incoming query, database
size, and estimated selectivity of the query. This is a prerequisite to later enhance the
query optimizer with cost models that take our processing system into account.
   The remainder of the article is outlined as follows: Section 2 discusses related work in
the field. Section 3 introduces the concept of the proposed SQL processing approach and
gives an overview of the methodology. The integration in an existing database man-
agement system (DBMS) is described in Section 4. The implemented module library
including all common SQL operations is introduced in Section 5, and the performance
calculus is presented in Section 6. A comparison between row- and column-wise pro-
cessing is the subject of Section 7, and the developed prototypes are introduced in
Section 8. Experimental results that compare our prototypes with software-only ap-
proaches and a comparison of the processing time of a query under different system
configurations are presented in Section 9. Finally, a conclusion is given in Section 10.
2. RELATED WORK
In this section, existing work on hardware acceleration of SQL query processing is
summarized. Netezza FAST engines [IBM 2014] is a commercially available platform
that uses FPGA support for query acceleration. It provides a static system with a
limited set of parameters, which only covered projection and restriction operators up
to now. Enhancing such a static system to support more operators leads to high area
requirements, regardless of whether the operators are used or not. Another approach is
provided by Glacier [Mueller et al. 2010], an SQL-to-VHDL compiler, which can compile
SQL queries into synthesizable VHDL. Other approaches accelerate specific database
operation, like hash-joins [Halstead et al. 2013] or the skyline operator [Woods et al.
2013]. Furthermore, FPGA-based XML filters [Teubner et al. 2013] might also help to
offload operations from a processor to an FPGA. Takenaka et al. [2012] showed how to
use FPGAs for SQL-based event processing. However, the need for a complete synthesis
makes all these approaches useful only for environments with a fixed and known set of
queries. Static hardware designs are inappropriate for two reasons: either they support
only a small set of query operators or the on-the-fly synthesis of query-specific designs
takes far too long.
   Configurable engines, as in IBM’s Netezza approach, might be a suitable compromise.
One example is the Ibex storage engine, which filters the incoming data with restriction
and aggregation operators implemented on an FPGA [Woods et al. 2014]. This filtering
engine is placed between the disks and the processor and efficiently reduces the data
volume that has to be processed by the processor. Another example is the system
proposed in Sukhwani et al. [2015], which covers restrictions and data sorting also with
the help of configurable engines. The reconfiguration of such engines for processing
multiple queries might be faster compared to our partial reconfiguration approach.
However, it restricts the flexibility of designing optimized modules for new operators
and, therefore, limits the extendability and efficiency of the system.
   Werner et al. [2013] analyzed different hardware implementations of joins used in
semantic web databases. They found the implementation of the merge-join to be the
fastest join variant. The analysis was done with stand-alone modules only. However, the
goal here is to provide join modules for a partially reconfigurable accelerator system.

ACM Transactions on Reconfigurable Technology and Systems, Vol. 9, No. 4, Article 25, Publication date: August 2016.
25:4                                                                                                D. Ziener et al.

  Finally, design flows supporting the design of partially reconfigurable systems are
summarized: Xilinx integrated the partial reconfiguration feature in their design tool
PlanAhead [Xilinx 2011]. Also, Altera supports partial reconfiguration for the new
Stratix V series and integrates a partial design flow in their tools that is quite similar
to the Xilinx approach [Bourgeault 2011]. However, all these approaches support only
an island reconfiguration style, which means that a partially reconfigurable module
can only be placed in one dedicated area and this area can only be occupied by a single
module at the same time. To overcome these restrictions, the FPGA research commu-
nity has introduced some partial design flows that are able to place several modules
into a partially reconfigurable area. Some of them allow even module relocation. The
approach proposed in the following also relies on one of such tools named GoAhead
[Beckhoff et al. 2012], which provides the generation of communication structures for
data-flow-oriented communications, as well as on the partial flow from Xilinx Plan-
Ahead.
3. CONCEPT AND SYSTEM OVERVIEW
In this section, we describe our concept of processing SQL operations using partial
dynamic reconfiguration. First, an overview of our system architecture is presented.
Next, a closer look at the basic architecture inside the FPGA is given.
   The major concept of on-the-fly query acceleration through partial dynamic FPGA
reconfiguration is depicted in Figure 1. An incoming query (see Listing 1) is analyzed by
an optimizer and the corresponding query execution plan is generated and processed by
a component called Reconfiguration Manager running on the host. Operator modules
from the module library, which reside in the main memory of the host, are selected and
the query data path is composed on the fly. After that, the streaming data path, which
typically cascades several modules, is loaded into a partially reconfigurable area inside
the FPGA. Furthermore, the reconfiguration manager keeps track of the allocation of
partially reconfigurable areas as well as active and finished queries.
   After module loading, the database tables are streamed from the main memory to
the FPGA and into the partially reconfigurable area. Hereby, the data is processed by
the loaded operator modules and the corresponding result is streamed continuously
back to the main memory. Each partially reconfigurable area may implement one
or a subset of a query accelerator, and each may consist of one or more partially
reconfigurable modules. Figure 1 shows also the partitioning of partially reconfigurable
areas into elementary units called slots forming a grid for the placement of modules.
Each module occupies one or more neighboring slots. Several concatenated modules
finally implement a specific query accelerator. The communication inside a partial
reconfigurable area between different modules is based on the I/O bar concept. An
I/O bar is a composition of several prerouted wires forming a data bus whose purpose
is to pipe a data stream. Partial modules can be plugged on and off the I/O bar at
runtime and have the possibility to bypass or manipulate the data stream. Such
communication structures can be built by using the GoAhead tool [Beckhoff et al.
2012] (see also Dennl et al. [2012] for more details).
   Inside the FPGA, tuples are processed in a fully pipelined manner by a chain of
modules. Usually, the bit width of a tuple is wider than the width of a communication
data bus and may even add up to several kilobytes. Thus, it is impossible to process
whole tuples at the speed of just one clock cycle. Therefore, tuples are divided into
smaller entities called chunks that match the data bus width and contain one or several
attributes. To achieve the best possible throughput, each module has been developed to
process one chunk per clock cycle. It may still have a latency of multiple clock cycles.
   Chunks must be properly sequenced (see Figure 2). Modules access exactly the at-
tributes needed for their operation by fetching the appropriate chunks from the data

  ACM Transactions on Reconfigurable Technology and Systems, Vol. 9, No. 4, Article 25, Publication date: August 2016.
FPGA-Based Dynamically Reconfigurable SQL Query Processing                                                        25:5




Fig. 1. An overview of the proposed query acceleration system: each incoming query is analyzed by the
Reconfiguration Manager and corresponding modules of the generated query execution plan are loaded
subsequently onto the FPGA. On the right, two partially reconfigurable areas are depicted that even allow
the simultaneous processing of two (partial) queries (Queries 1 and 2) in parallel.




                                    Listing 1. Two incoming example queries.




Fig. 2. Snapshot of processing tuples. In the example, tuples consist of three attributes and three chunks,
and the modules are configured with indices that denote the position of the operands. The shown data path
consists of three cascaded modules. It is not determined yet how the results are handled. Figure 3 shows the
completed snapshot.

stream. Each chunk has a unique index and the modules are configured with the right
chunk indices; for example, if an adder module needs chunks 2 and 4 as inputs, it is
configured with index 2 for the first operand and with index 4 for the second. Each
module counts the bypassing chunks and loads its operand registers when the right
chunk arrives.
  The modules are also configured with the number of chunks per tuple. Thus, a module
recognizes when a tuple ends and a new tuple begins. This information is important
because projections and restrictions are evaluated row-wise; that is, each tuple is
evaluated independently. Operands not only are attributes but also can be configured
as constant values. As stated earlier, attributes must be included in single chunks
in order to address them via indices. Figure 2 shows a snapshot of a typical data-
processing stream. The modules are configured with the appropriate chunk indices,
which denote the position of the operands inside the tuple.

ACM Transactions on Reconfigurable Technology and Systems, Vol. 9, No. 4, Article 25, Publication date: August 2016.
25:6                                                                                                 D. Ziener et al.




Fig. 3. Adjusting the data processing introduced in Figure 2 to handle intermediate results. Spare chunks
are appended to the end of each tuple to provide space for intermediate results.




Fig. 4. The query will be analyzed by an optimizer that generates a (partial) execution plan. The corre-
sponding modules are selected, configured, and placed by the reconfiguration manager. Finally, the modules
are loaded onto the FPGA and the query is beginning to be processed.

   To include intermediate results in the tuple stream, a sufficient number of spare
chunks per tuple is allocated in advance. The modules are then configured with the
proper result index. Hence, each module knows where it has to insert its results.
Figure 3 shows an adjusted tuple-stream processing. Modules are configured with an
additional result index.
   The minimum number of spare chunks, the assignment to intermediate results, and
the placement order of operator modules inside the partially reconfigurable area from
left to right can be determined by using query expression trees with posttraversal lin-
earization. A more detailed description of these tasks can be found in Dennl et al. [2012].
   The proposed partially reconfigurable areas are perfectly suited for streaming-based
operations with one input port and one output port, like restrictions and aggregations.
However, operations like joins need at least two input ports (the two tables), and many
SQL operations have to store intermediate results in an external memory, like sorting
or the usage of large hash tables. In order to also support such kind of operations, an ad-
ditional partially reconfigurable area with two input ports, one output port, and access
to an external DDR memory is proposed. This partially reconfigurable area supports
only the configuration of a single module per time. In Section 8, the architecture of dif-
ferent prototyping systems using a mixture of streaming-based partially reconfigurable
areas and such a multiple-port partially reconfigurable area is described.

4. DATABASE MANAGEMENT SYSTEM INTEGRATION
For practical use, it is of the utmost importance to integrate the SQL accelerator into an
existing DBMS. The user inputs a query to the database management system (DBMS)
and the optimizer decides which parts of the query are to be executed on the host
and which are to be offloaded to the FPGA (see Figure 4). The optimizer has statistics
on the requested data and tables and has the knowledge about the feasibility and
limitations to execute certain operators on the FPGA. If hardware acceleration of a

   ACM Transactions on Reconfigurable Technology and Systems, Vol. 9, No. 4, Article 25, Publication date: August 2016.
FPGA-Based Dynamically Reconfigurable SQL Query Processing                                                        25:7

query or subquery is chosen, the module assembly and reconfiguration manager takes
care of that portion of the query execution plan and selects the appropriate partially
reconfigurable modules along with their correct initialization parameters. The locations
in the partially reconfigurable areas are determined and the FPGA will be reconfigured
over the so-called internal configuration access port (ICAP). The location inside a partial
reconfigurable area depends on the needed slot type (only CLBs, CLB + BRAMs, or
CLB + DSP slices) and the operator location on the query plan. After the module
reconfiguration, the module parameters are sent from the host to the corresponding
modules. The accelerator is now ready to process the data. The incoming tables are
streamed through the partially reconfigurable area and the results are transferred
back to the host. In some cases, iterations over the accelerator board are necessary with
intermediate module reconfiguration. As soon as the entire query has been processed,
the result is presented to the user.
   A possible system architecture is described in the following: multiple hard drives
storing the database are attached to the host PC via a SATA interface. Data transfers
between host and FPGA are done using DMA support on the host’s main memory.
The database tables stored on the disks are transferred to the main memory and
are streamed from there to the FPGA over the communication interface. After the
hardware query processing, the FPGA stores the (partial) results in main memory for
further processing.
   The limiting factor of this architecture is the communication bottleneck between
the disks, main memory, and FPGA. Therefore, to increase the overall throughput,
an improved architecture would attach the disks directly to the FPGA, as in Woods
et al. [2014], to avoid or allay this bottleneck in future systems. In this case, the data
is streamed from the disks immediately into the FPGA. However, a SATA controller
must then be implemented on the accelerator board.
   In general, this approach is independent of the type of data and control communica-
tion interface. Over the control interface, the partial bit files are loaded and configured.
The table data to the FPGA and the results from the FPGA are transferred over the
data interface. In Dennl et al. [2013], a PCI-Express (PCIe) connection to the host is
used to implement both interfaces. In Becher et al. [2014], an energy-aware processing
platform is presented that utilizes AXI interfaces for the communication with two ARM
cores (see also Section 8).
   The way that data are organized and stored on disk or in the memory is very im-
portant for the data processing and has a high impact on the overall performance of
the DBMS. Traditionally, databases store the tables row by row. An alternative way of
storing the data is column-wise. This latter approach has been investigated in recent
years [Stonebraker et al. 2005] and has shown a significant increase in performance
for query execution on some workloads. Therefore, our proposed accelerating system
supports both types of data processing (see Section 7).
5. THE MODULE LIBRARY
In the following, we present the operator library that has been designed for our hard-
ware accelerator. The highly optimized modules form a very flexible library of recon-
figurable hardware modules. Currently, the library consists of modules for processing
restrictions, including arithmetics (+,−,∗), comparators (<,>,=,=), and bitwise func-
tions (AND, OR, NOT, XOR, NAND, NOR); aggregations (SUM, MIN, MAX, COUNT);
merge-join; hash-join; sort; and a module that reorders, removes, or adds attributes
within a tuple. All modules have a uniform interface. The restriction and aggregation
modules are described in detail in Dennl et al. [2012] and Dennl et al. [2013], the
merge-join, sort, and reorder module in Becher et al. [2014]. Most modules can be used
likewise for row- and column-based processing. Only a few modules are optimized for
processing data column-wise by using a late materialization strategy (see Section 7.3).
ACM Transactions on Reconfigurable Technology and Systems, Vol. 9, No. 4, Article 25, Publication date: August 2016.
25:8                                                                                                 D. Ziener et al.

5.1. Restriction
Restriction denotes a group of modules that can handle most of the operations specified
in the WHERE clause of an SQL query. This includes arithmetic, comparison, and logical
operations, which are implemented in several modules, one for each operation. The
positions of the operands and of the result are configurable. Most modules also support a
configurable constant as one of the operands. We designed modules for comparison, bit-
wise operations, and arithmetic operations, as well as a module for string comparison.
For more information, see Dennl et al. [2012].
  The restriction modules only mark the tuples, but do not remove them from the
stream. This is left to a module called Reorder, which will be introduced and described
in detail in Section 5.3.

5.2. Aggregation
Aggregations like SUM() or MAX() are operations to compute statistical results for
multiple tuples of a table. In this work, we consider only the following aggregation
functions, because they are very common in databases: SUM(), MIN(), and MAX(). Op-
tionally, aggregations can be combined with a GROUP BY clause to compute aggregated
values for groups of tuples, which are defined by the values of one or more attributes
specified in the clause. The difference between single-column and multicolumn group-
ing is in fact a minor one, because technically multicolumn grouping only results in a
higher number of groups, and the grouping attribute is just a compound key. For ag-
gregations without grouping, only the position of the affected attribute inside a tuple
and chunk is needed. As soon as the entire table has been processed, the aggregated
value has also been computed and can be appended directly to the end of the stream.
   If the aggregation is combined with grouping, more than one value must be computed.
We need one for each group. Two different approaches can be used to support grouping,
each having different advantages and drawbacks.
   The first possibility to compute grouped aggregations is the use of hash functions to
compute memory addresses for the values of each group. For module implementation,
the only memory type that is currently available in partially reconfigurable modules
is Block-RAM. Partial reconfiguration allows to use different memory configurations,
for example, smaller address ranges but wider data types (important for SUM()), or
larger address ranges but smaller data types (sufficient for, e.g., MAX()). With the help
of partial reconfigurability, it is also possible to provide a whole bunch of different
hash functions for different situations. A big advantage of the hash-based approach,
however, is that no tuple sorting is needed; that is, the tuple stream can be processed
in the given order.
   The second approach is a sorting-based approach, where the tuples of the input table
are sorted by their respective group keys. They either are presorted in the table or can be
sorted on the FPGA by using the modules SortLine and SortTree (see Section 5.6). After
sorting, one group arrives after the other. Thus, as soon as one group has been streamed
through, the aggregated value is completed and is sent on along with the group. This
way, only one value must be stored at a time, which completely annihilates the necessity
of Block-RAM inside partially reconfigurable modules. Furthermore, the limitation of
group counts does not exist anymore. However, the biggest drawback of this approach
is sorting. Sorting large amounts of data inside FPGAs is a very resource-intensive
task. For more details about the sorting-based approach, see Dennl et al. [2013].

5.3. Reorder
In Section 3, it was shown that tuples that do not fit on the width of the partially
reconfigurable area must be cut into chunks. Attributes may be a part of a chunk,

   ACM Transactions on Reconfigurable Technology and Systems, Vol. 9, No. 4, Article 25, Publication date: August 2016.
FPGA-Based Dynamically Reconfigurable SQL Query Processing                                                        25:9




Fig. 5. Concept and structure of a Reorder module with a 128-bit interface–data-path control part. Chunks
are cut into the 32-bit-wide slices S0, S1, S2, and S3, respectively. After passing through a switching network
that reorders these slices according to an input signal provided by the current instruction, each slice is stored
in a local 32-bit-wide Block-RAM. The current_instruction holds four individual addresses to read data back
from the Block-RAMs, and another switching network allows one to change the slice order once again. An
out_en signal indicates whether the data produced by the current instructions is valid or not.


but may also use more then one chunk, as is often the case with string attributes. A
reordering of the attributes inside of tuples is needed to move attributes to the positions
where subsequent modules can process them. Modules also need spare chunks to insert
intermediate results or even attribute duplication, for example, to complete a join
operation with tuple size greater then one chunk (see Section 5.4). For these tuple
manipulations, we introduce a new module that reorders the attributes of tuples. In
contrast to prior work such as the stream permutation work of Milder et al. [2009],
we use an instruction-based approach and two switch networks instead of one. This
is simple and saving Block-RAMs as these would increase the size of this module and
therefore decrease flexibility within partial reconfiguration. Furthermore, due to the
instruction-based approach, which also allows for branches and conditional branches
based on input data, it not only removes unneeded attributes to save bandwidth for
following modules, but also gives the opportunity for data-dependent tuple removal.
   To accomplish this, each chunk is cut into equal-width slices, taking a practical size
of 32 bits, as most data are aligned to that anyway. Dual-ported Block-RAMs are used
to store the slices of all chunks of an incoming tuple, each at an individual address (see
Figure 5). A switch network can change the order of the slices before they are written
to the Block-RAMs. On the output part, the module can read from four independent
addresses and reorder the slices again to build a new valid chunk. This allows one
to reorder, duplicate, and remove one or more attributes from the stream as long as
they are aligned with the chosen slice width. The addresses and switch networks are
controlled by Very Large Instruction Words (VLIWs) stored in the instruction Block-
RAM. Figure 5 shows how the data is controlled by the data-path control part of the
current instruction. These VLIWs allow us not only to process each chunk in just one
clock cycle, but also to add control-flow support. This means that each incoming chunk
of a tuple has at least one individual instruction. More information about the Reorder
module can be found in Becher et al. [2014].

5.4. MergeJoin
The join operator is highly important in modern relational databases. We have im-
plemented a fast way of joining two tables using our stream-based architecture to
further increase the number of operations supported by our acceleration framework.
To avoid high resource consumption, a merge-join algorithm is used. It is restricted to

ACM Transactions on Reconfigurable Technology and Systems, Vol. 9, No. 4, Article 25, Publication date: August 2016.
25:10                                                                                                D. Ziener et al.




Fig. 6. Example to show how our implementation of a join works. Dark arrows mark the active data path,
whereas light ones are switched off. For easier understanding, only the key values of each chunk are shown.
After loading the first chunk of each table into built-in registers (Subfigures 1 and 2), they are compared with
each other. Since the key value of the left (upper) chunk is smaller, l_enable is set to load the next chunk of
the left table. In Subfigure 4, the two key values are now equal, which results in the output of the left chunk
and a request for a new one. Also, the key value of the left table is stored in an internal spare register for
later use. After the left table chunk has been sent to the output, the right table follows, and the next chunk
is requested here as well (Subfigure 5). Subfigure 5 also shows the case of equality with the saved key value,
resulting in the output of the saved chunk of the left table. After the chunk from the right table has been
forwarded to the output, the inverse behavior can be observed in Subfigures 3 to 8.



one-to-many joins at the moment, but this is known to be the most important case.
Figure 6 shows how the join merges two sorted input streams into an output stream
by controlling a multiplexer (called left and right in the figure).
   With the use of a spare register (dotted squares in Figure 6), our design supports
one-to-many joins, as long as one tuple does not consist of more than one chunk. A
Reorder module as introduced in Section 5.3 that is used afterwards, for example, to
strip off no longer needed attributes, can also reconstruct missing chunks from 1:n
joins by copying them. This eliminates the one-chunk-only limitation.
   For this stream-based merge-join approach to work, the tables must be sorted by the
join keys. Today, most of the large tables are sorted anyway by the attribute mostly
used in joins, or they are indexed accordingly with the option to read the index in
sort-order (e.g., B+-tree). Restrictions may also filter incoming data before they enter
the join module. For the resulting smaller amounts of data, we propose a fast SortLine
module, which will be presented in Section 5.6. Another prerequisite of our approach is
that the key attribute must be in the first chunk of a tuple to limit the amount of data
stored inside the join module. Once again, a reorder unit can resolve that limitation.
   A left outer join outputs the complete left table and adds a tuple from the right table,
if a common key value is found. This behavior can be evoked by treating a smaller (<)

   ACM Transactions on Reconfigurable Technology and Systems, Vol. 9, No. 4, Article 25, Publication date: August 2016.
FPGA-Based Dynamically Reconfigurable SQL Query Processing                                                      25:11




Fig. 7. The HASHJoin Module with the HASH table and the Data table. The keys {1, 15, 4, 9, 7} were
inserted in this order.

in the first comparison of Figure 6 also as an equal (=), but creating empty chunks
instead of forwarding the right table.

5.5. HashJoin
For increasing the flexibility of our database accelerator system, a module for hash-
based joins was implemented and will be described in this section. Databases using
the Star Schema on which a single large table is joined with many small tables benefit
from the so called hash-join. In contrast to the previously introduced merge-join, this
implementation does not require any correctly sorted tables as inputs. It utilizes hash
tables for fast lookups of matching join attributes. This might lead to a much faster
join operation. One important goal for implementing a hash-join is finding a good hash
function that minimizes the likelihood of collisions. This can be achieved by selecting
a function that will result in evenly distributed hash values over the whole set of
resulting hash values. As the most common join attribute is some sort of numeric
identifier (ID), a simple modulo function is suitable as the hash function and will be
used here.
   The actual implementation of the HashJoin module consists of two entities, namely,
HASH table and Data table. The HASH table is a real hash table that holds a bit to
indicate if an entry is valid (hit bit) and a corresponding address for the Data table.
The Data table stores, depending on its configuration, one whole chunk of data or an
address for the DDR interface. Furthermore, to allow chaining inside the table, a NEXT
address that points to the following entry is stored in each entry of the Data table. This
way, the collisions are resolved as equal hash values lead to multiple, individual entries
in the Data table. If this NEXT address is 0, it is considered the last element of this list.
A negative value means that the address counts from the last memory location down
to the first one. The value −1, for example, would be the last entry in the Data table.
With this addressing scheme, it is possible to have all first entries of these lists at the
beginning of the Data table. Probing just these values would result in a GROUP-BY
function if collisions can be disregarded.
   Figure 7 shows the block diagram of the implemented HashJoin with its connections
to the DDR3 interface and the control signals read, store, and get. The store signal

ACM Transactions on Reconfigurable Technology and Systems, Vol. 9, No. 4, Article 25, Publication date: August 2016.
25:12                                                                                                D. Ziener et al.

triggers the Data table to insert the current KEY—which is the join attribute—into
the list. If an entry is already present at the given address, it is moved to the next free
address of the table counted backward (negative address) and the new KEY with its
corresponding DDR address (DDR-ADDR) is inserted. Once the first table is completely
streamed, the get signal comes into play. It is active if a hashed key from the second
table finds a match inside the HASH table. The Data table will then output the whole
list starting at the address stored in the HASH table in sequential order after each
clock cycle. The equal symbol compares the key from table two with the one stored in
the Data table. If it matches, the join is successful and the read signal is sent to the
DDR interface to read the data from the address (DDR-ADDR) stored inside the Data
table.
5.6. Sort
Sorting is one of the most processing-intensive parts of a query; thus, it is important
to have a fast hardware acceleration. Our dynamic accelerator system is based on a
sorter concept described in Koch and Torresen [2011]. It consists of the following two
modules:
   The SortLine is the first sorting module that is responsible for presorting blocks with
the size of a few kilobytes. It needs no access to an external memory and fully relies on
on-chip distributed RAM and Block-RAM. It cannot sort large datasets, only fixed-sized
blocks. The big advantage of the SortLine is that it is fully pipelined, so it can process
one chunk each cycle. This module consists of multiple stages. Stage i requires memory
to store 2i chunks. A SortLine of k stages can sort blocks of 2k chunks.
   The sorted blocks can then be processed by the second sorting module, the SortTree.
The SortTree merges the presorted blocks to a fully sorted table by using external
memory. The external memory is necessary to be able to sort large blocks of data. The
SortTree module is not fully pipelined. It may need multiple iterations i to sort the
entire data. It consists of an n-depth tree that sorts 2n blocks of any size. For example,
a three-deep SortTree feed with 64kB sorted blocks from the SortLine produces 512kB
blocks in a single iteration. In the second iteration, the result would be sorted in blocks
of 4MB.
5.7. BitVector
To process data using late materialization (see Section 7.3 for details), a list of required
rows must be returned from the accelerator to the CPU. This could be a list of primary
keys, but that would consume too much bandwidth—not only on the return path,
because the primary key must have been sent to the accelerator in the first place. As
all columns are stored in the same order, one bit per row is enough to provide the
information.
  The implemented module looks for the result of the restriction in each input tuple and
saves it as 1 bit of a vector. Once 128 values are stored, an output chunk is generated.
When an end-of-file signal is received, the remaining bits of the current vector are filled
with zeroes and the vector is written to the output. The input tuple itself is discarded
by the module.
5.8. ColumnJoin
The ColumnJoin module is used for column-based query processing only. As columns
are stored separately from each other, there must be a way to rejoin them again,
for cases where multiple columns are required to execute an operation, that is, for
materialization of (parts of) tuples.
  The ColumnJoin module does an implicit join of multiple columns without needing
a key. The columns are joined 1 : 1 : 1 : ... based on the positions. That is, the nth

   ACM Transactions on Reconfigurable Technology and Systems, Vol. 9, No. 4, Article 25, Publication date: August 2016.
FPGA-Based Dynamically Reconfigurable SQL Query Processing                                                      25:13

value of the first column is joined with the nth value of the second column. It is not
allowed that columns are sorted or filtered before joining; otherwise, the orderings
would be inconsistent. The module starts to emit data to the remainder of the partially
reconfigurable area after one block of each column has arrived. The module is placed
at the start of the partially reconfigurable area and needs memory to store two blocks
of each column. This allows to produce output while at the same time receiving
input.

6. A CALCULUS FOR PERFORMANCE ASSESSMENT
In this section, a calculus for the performance assessment of query processing in our
system is introduced. The goal and purpose of this calculus is to be able to evaluate
which parameters influence the achievable throughput and latency of query processing
in which way. These parameters could be clock frequency, number of modules, bit-
widths, and other hardware parameters.
  In order to analyze the throughput of the acceleration system, the processing delay
d of a chunk (measured in nanoseconds) and the throughput D of each module as
well as that of the input and output interfaces are determined. Due to our pipelined
architecture, most of the modules have a constant throughput of one chunk per clock
cycle. By taking the bus width of a partially reconfigurable area widthpa and the clock
frequency fclock, a throughput Dpa of widthpa · fclock can be achieved.
  In addition to the delay of chunks and throughput of each module, the total execution
time texec also depends on the number of tuples T to process and on the size C of a tuple
(measured in chunks). These two values are not constant and might be different from
module to module. Thus, we use a 4-tuple (d, D, T , C) to describe the behavior each
module. It depends on the intrinsics of the module as well as the previous component
in the pipeline, or in case of the join, on the two inputs. The first component is always
the input interface from the host. The total execution time can be therefore calculated
from the 4-tuple of the last module in the chain:
                                                       Clast · Tlast · widthpa
                                    texec = dlast +                            .                                       (1)
                                                                 Dlast
  The path from the main memory of the host to the FPGA and back cannot be exactly
captured by formulas. The driver, cache hierarchies, interrupts, multiple CPU cores,
and components sharing a bus all together make the system too complex and indeter-
ministic. For this reason, a maximum throughput is measured on the system using a
single empty partially reconfigurable area. It must be taken into account that the input
and output streams may share one medium.

6.1. Performance Assessment of Library Modules
For each module type, the formulas to calculate the 4-tuple of the output (dout , Dout ,
Tout , Cout ) are presented in Table I. As input vector (din, Din, Tin, Cin), the output vector
of the previous module in the chain is used. The join modules use two input vectors
(in1, in2), one for each input stream.
   For our prototypical implementation (see Section 8), the latency l of the corresponding
module in clock cycles is set for restrictions and aggregations to lRestr = l Aggr = 3, for
the Reorder module to lReorder = 6, for the MergeJoin module to lMerge Join = 6, for the
ColumnJoin module to lColumnJoin = 5, and for the BitVector module to lBitV ector = 4.
The latency of the kline -stage SortLine module can be calculated as follows: lSortLine =
2kline +1 + 3 · kline − 2 . The Reorder module filters tuples that are marked for removal from
previous restrictions with a selectivity 0 ≥ s ≥ 1 and truncates unneeded attributes.
The latter has a high impact on the number of output chunks Cnew .

   The hash-join performance assessment is simplified. The hash-join latency lHashJoin
and throughput DHashJoin depend on the collision rate, the latency for resolving colli-
sions, and the latency for reading values from the external DDR memory. The selectivity
mj of the join can be calculated with mj = Tout /(Tin1 · Tin2 ).

iteration lSortT ree depends on the implementation of the module itself and the controller
of the external memory. Dmem denotes the available data throughput to the external
memory. The data rate Dpart1 for calculating the overall throughput of the MergeJoin
can be calculated as follows:

                                                                       Cin1 + Cin2

  The ColumnJoin module joins col columns and sizeblock is the size of a single block
sent from the CPU. The width of the join attribute is widthattr . The compression rate
cr of the BitVector module can be calculated with cr = 1/(widthpa · Cin).

6.2. Performance Assessment of an Example Query
To calculate the execution time of a full query, the formulas for the individual modules
must be combined. This is done step by step starting from the input. This output of
one module is the input for the next one. The latencies are simply summed up and give
the time from the first tuple moving to the accelerator to the first tuple arriving at
the output. Modules in the partially reconfigurable area not only add latency but also
may change the amount of data and the rate of data output. A simple example query
is introduced in Listing 2 to show how the execution time calculation works.
   The table has 365 entries (Tdays ) and each row has a size of 26 bytes, requiring two
chunks (Cdays ) for a 128-bit partially reconfigurable area architecture. The query can be
processed by a Restriction module followed by a Reorder module. The steps to calculate
the 4-tuple for each module are shown in Table II. The last column can then be used to

7. ROW-BASED VERSUS COLUMN-BASED PROCESSING
Traditionally, databases store the tables row by row. However, for many queries, a
significant increase in performance is achieved if the data is processed column-wise
(see, for instance, Stonebraker et al. [2005]). In the following, different strategies are
proposed to execute an example query based on the TPC-DS benchmark [Council 2012]
(see Listing 3). This query is used as a representative example, which will be used for
the remainder of this article.




                 Listing 3. An SQL query based on the TPC-DS benchmark is used for evaluation.


7.1. Row-Based Query Processing
The strategy for processing the query with traditional row-based storage is discussed
first. In this setup, the input to the first partially reconfigurable area is always a full
table (or the intermediate result of a prior run). This may be a huge amount of data;
thus, the idea is to first remove as much data as possible. This is done by applying all
restrictions that affect only the current input table and then using a Reorder module
(introduced in Section 5) to apply the filter and to remove all columns not needed for
the remainder of the query. This can easily result in a reduction of the input data by a
factor of 100 or more. The following join has only to process the remaining data. The
query plan for row-based processing is given in Figure 8.

ACM Transactions on Reconfigurable Technology and Systems, Vol. 9, No. 4, Article 25, Publication date: August 2016.
25:16                                                                                                D. Ziener et al.




Fig. 8. Plan for row-based execution of the query depicted in Listing 3. Circles represent data sources or
sinks. The modules are displayed using the symbols. The symbol  denotes the Reorder module. Arrows
represent data flow. Involved tables/attributes/constants are shown above or below the nodes.




Fig. 9. Plan for column-based execution of the query depicted in Listing 3 using early materialization. Circles
represent data sources or sinks. The modules are displayed using the symbols. The symbol  denotes the
Reorder module. Arrows represent data flow. Involved tables/attributes/constants are shown above or below
the nodes.

7.2. Column-Based Query Processing: Early Materialization
The strategy for column-based storage with early materialization is similar to the
row-based approach. The idea of early materialization is to join the columns at the
beginning of the processing to reconstruct the (parts of the) tuples that are required for
the execution of a particular query [Abadi et al. 2008]. After that, all modules developed
for row-based storage can be used.
  Instead of loading the full table and then filtering with the Reorder module, we only
load the required columns using the ColumnJoin module introduced in Section 5. One
Reorder module can be skipped, as its only job was removing columns. The resulting
plan is shown in Figure 9.

7.3. Column-Based Query Processing: Late Materialization
Late materialization [Abadi et al. 2008] is an approach that tries to execute the query
with the columns retrieved from storage as far as possible and only materialize tuples
when required for output to the user. Thus, data (in the form of columns) is loaded as
late as possible, which minimizes the transfer data to the board. Using the current ar-
chitecture, this results in many inexpensive subexpressions executed one after another
by the accelerator.
   Late materialization also requires random access to the data, because other at-
tributes of the tuple at hand can be stored at different positions in their column struc-
ture. That cannot be achieved with a streaming accelerator. The accelerator, therefore,
generates bit-vectors that contain a list of the required rows. The CPU gathers these

   ACM Transactions on Reconfigurable Technology and Systems, Vol. 9, No. 4, Article 25, Publication date: August 2016.
FPGA-Based Dynamically Reconfigurable SQL Query Processing                                                      25:17




Fig. 10. Plan for column-based execution of the query depicted in Listing 3 using late materialization. Circles
represent data sources or sinks. The modules are displayed using the symbols. The symbol  denotes the
Reorder module. Arrows represent data flow. Involved tables/attributes/constants are shown above or below
the nodes. The figure only shows the parts executed on the accelerator.


values and streams them back to the accelerator. This happens in parallel to the exe-
cution on the accelerator, so the overhead is acceptable.
  Figure 10 shows a possible execution plan for the example query using late materi-
alization. There are many different ways to execute it. Which to prefer highly depends
on the data and the available resources. One scenario is to load the three different
independent query plan parts depicted in Figure 10 sequentially on the query process-
ing system by using partial reconfiguration and storing the intermediate results in
the main memory. A mixture of early and late materialization may be appropriate to
balance storage I/O and the number of executed subqueries.

8. PROTOTYPES
We have prototyped our partially reconfigurable query accelerator engine on a Xilinx
ML605 board, which includes a Virtex-6 XC6VLX240T FPGA and two boards based
on the Xilinx Zynq SoC (Zedboard and Xilinx ZC706 board). For reasons of flexibility,
we have decided to segment the reconfigurable fabric into a static system consisting
of four partially reconfigurable areas, a PCIe controller for the ML605 board and AXI
controllers for the Zynq boards, and a hardware part of the reconfiguration manager to
configure the system (see Figure 11). The latter is responsible for loading the respective
partially reconfigurable modules over ICAP, for configuring the module parameters,
and for configuring the interface between the communication interface (PCIe or AXI)
and the partially reconfigurable areas. Four partially reconfigurable areas have been
chosen to be able to process four queries at the same time. Alternatively, the partially
reconfigurable areas can be concatenated to support queries with higher processing
depth.
   Finally, each partially reconfigurable area is divided into 16 slots with each slot
having a height of 40 CLBs and a width of 2 CLBs, or a 1-CLB and 1-DSP/BRAM
unit (see Figure 12). Thus, one slot contains 640 or 1,280 flip-flops and 320 or 640
LUTs. Table III shows the resource usage of the different partially reconfigurable
modules on Virtex-6. Furthermore, each reconfigurable area has a 128-bit data bus.

ACM Transactions on Reconfigurable Technology and Systems, Vol. 9, No. 4, Article 25, Publication date: August 2016.
25:18                                                                                                D. Ziener et al.

figuration manager, and the host memory containing the database and the operation library are depicted.

munication interface, and the control modules are shown.

Fig. 13. The query from Listing 3 requires three Reorders (reo), two Restrictions (res), one MergeJoin, and
one Aggregation (aggr) module. In this figure, we see how the modules are placed. The table date_dim is
streamed to reconfigurable area 1, where the first and second restriction filter for d_moy = 11 AND d_year =
2000 reside. Before the two data streams enter the MergeJoin, one Reorder module before each join input
strips off not needed attributes. The joined table enters the aggregation to sum ext_sales_price and another
reorder unit moves the attributes so the output matches the selected format of the query.

The system operates at 125MHz on the Virtex-6, 150MHz on the Zedboard, and 175MHz
on the ZC706, which delivers a total throughput of 2GB/s, 2.4GB/s, and 2.8GB/s per
reconfigurable area, respectively. Therefore, loading all four reconfigurable areas with
independent queries leads to a theoretical maximum throughput of 8GB/s, 9.6GB/s,
or 11.2GB/s, respectively. The PCIe Gen2 bus with four lanes can only provide a net
transfer rate of 1.7GB/s for each direction; that is, the bus is clearly the bottleneck in
this setup. The SoCs consist of a dual-core ARM Cortex A9 clocked at 666MHz and
an FPGA fabric. The partially reconfigurable areas are connected to the ARM and the
DDR memory via AXI-DMA cores with 64-bit data width. The two high-performance
ports run at a clock frequency of 175MHz. One general-purpose AXI-lite bus is used to
control the DMA cores. On the software side, we use a Linaro-Ubuntu 14.02 distribution
running a Linux 3.12.0-xilinx kernel.

9. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS
In the following, we compare our prototypes with software implementations. Further-
more, we show that our performance assessment calculus presented in Section 6 is
quite accurate. The overhead introduced by partial reconfiguration is shown, and with
the help of the performance assessment, the processing time of different processing
strategies (row-wise or column-wise) is shown for different table sizes.
  As a representative example, an accelerator for the query depicted in Listing 3 in
Section 7 is used. In order to map the whole query to our accelerator system, we need to
instantiate two Restriction modules, one Aggregation module, three Reorder modules,
and a MergeJoin module. The corresponding placement of the modules in the partially
reconfigurable areas of our platform is shown in Figure 13.

9.1. Comparison to Software-Only Approaches
We compare our proposed prototypes with software-only solutions running on an x86-
based server and on the ARM cores of the ZedBoard. Furthermore, a comparison of
the different prototypes is presented. For the ARM and x86-based software-only con-
figuration, we use a MySQL installation each with INMEMORY tables to neglect the
I/O traffic from the hard disc or SD card, respectively. Our x86-based server system
is running Arch Linux with a 3.7.9 kernel on an Intel Core i7-3770 CPU clocked at
3.4GHz and 16GB DDR3 memory. The ML605-based system is connected to our x86
server over PCIe Gen2 using four lanes. Note that the throughput and latency of all

streaming-based partial areas are absolutely deterministic. Therefore, we choose only
some selected scenarios to back up our performance assessment. In addition to the
processing of the query in Listing 3 by using a merge join on the Zedboard, we process
the query and some derivations, shown in Listing 4, on the ZC706 board by using the
hash-join, which utilizes the external memory.
  Table IV shows the processing time texec of the queries in Listing 4 on our proposed
prototypes calculated using the throughput analysis presented in Section 6 and real
measured values. Furthermore, the execution time of software-only approaches using
MySQL on the x86-based server and the embedded ARM core are given. All these
results are obtained for the TPC-DS database with the scale factor of 1GB. For the
throughput analysis, we measure an AXI-interface throughput of 1.2GB/s for the Zed-
board and 2.77GB/s for the ZC706 board. For the PCIe Gen2 connection with four
lanes, we assumed a throughput of 1.7GB/s. To emphasize the benefits of our approach
regarding energy consumption, we include measurement in each individual query in
Table IV. For determining the energy consumption, the system power on query pro-
cessing and the idle power are measured. The shown energy values include only the
additional energy for query processing. Note that the idle power of the x86 system is
32.7W compared to 12.4W for the ZC706 board and 3.6W for the Zedboard.




   Listing 4. SQL queries for evaluation based on the query in Listing 3 (Q1 is the query in Listing 3).


  It can be seen that both accelerated embedded Zynq-based systems and the ML605
prototype are faster than the MySQL-based x86-system even if a reconfiguration over-
head of 1.88ms (see Section 9.2) is included in order to load the partially reconfigurable
modules initially. However, an optimized C++ solution on the x86 platform would out-
perform our solution due to a much higher memory bandwidth (see Becher et al. [2014]
for details). It can be seen that for Zynq targets, our presented analytic formula-based
query execution time determination is quite accurate. Finally, the experimental results
give evidence that the proposed architecture, especially on the low-power Zedboard,
may reduce the amount of consumed energy significantly compared to the energy
needed by an in-memory database system running on an x86-based server at equal
throughput.

9.2. Overhead Introduced by Partial Reconfiguration
The partial dynamic reconfiguration process utilizes one of the configuration ports
of the FPGA. In our approach, we are using the internal configuration access port
(ICAP), which makes the configuration memory accessible from the FPGA fabric. The
ICAP interface of the Xilinx Virtex-6 and Zynq has a data width of 32 bits and can
by clocked up to 100MHz, which results in a maximal configuration throughput of
400MB/s. Furthermore, there exist some approaches to overclock the configuration
interface in order to achieve a higher configuration speed [Claus et al. 2010].
   The second parameter, which influences the configuration speed, is the interface
between the host and the FPGA board. Since the partial bit files are stored on the
filesystem of the host, the bit files have to be transferred to the FPGA. The transfer
rates of the PCIe interface of the ML605 board and the AXI interfaces of the Zynq boards
are higher than the 400MB/s of the configuration interface. Therefore, the bottleneck
is the limitation of the ICAP. Table V presents the module loading time of different
module sizes.
9.3. Overall Performance Assessment
In order to evaluate the overall performance of our approach, the database scheme and
corresponding table data from the TPC-DS benchmark [Council 2012] are used. As a
representative query, the query in Listing 3 is taken for this analysis. The performance
estimation is done by using our model for performance assessment, described in
Section 6, with the performance models of the corresponding modules, described in
Section 5.
   For this evaluation, we use our prototype, based on the Xilinx Virtex-6 ML605-
board (see Section 8). For the interface throughput, we estimate a realistic throughput
of 1.7GB/s, whereas the throughput of the on-board DDR3 interface is 12GB/s. The
partially reconfigurable areas are 128 bits wide and are clocked with 125MHz, which
results in an overall throughput of 2GB/s for each partially reconfigurable area.
   The performance of the query in Listing 3 is analyzed by using a row-based (see Sec-
tion 7.1) and two different column-based processing approaches. The first one is early
materialization (see Section 7.2) and the second is late materialization (see Section 7.3).
Each of these processing scenarios is further evaluated by using sort-merge-join and
hash-join approaches. The sort-merge-join approaches are subdivided into two cases.
The first case assumes that the tables are presorted, so only the merge-join is processed
on the FPGA. In the second case, the tables must be sorted on the FPGA before the
merge-join can be processed. The results are shown in Table VI for different benchmark
database scales and depicted in Figure 14.
   It can be seen that the processing time rises linearly with the database size. Further-
more, the significant improvement by utilizing column processing can also be seen. The

Fig. 14. The results for the performance assessment of the query shown in Listing 3 and different TPC-DS
benchmark [Council 2012] database scales for row-based processing (RS) and column-based processing by
using early materialization (EM) and late materialization (LM). This figure shows the results from the merge-
join with sorting (sort-merge-join) and the processing with presorted tables with the merge-join (merge-join)
as well as the processing time by utilizing the hash-join module.

difference between early and late materialization is almost negligible due to the very
small dimension table date_dim. The TPC-DS benchmark scales only the fact table
store_sales and not the dimension tables. Furthermore, by applying the restrictions on
the dimension table, only 30 entries are left for the join, which is further independent
of the database scale. By comparing the different join variants, the hash-join has al-
most the same processing time as the merge-join without sorting. Sorting introduces
a significant latency increase. Furthermore, for sorting large tables, a huge amount
of on-board memory is needed. For example, for processing the fact table of the 1TB
database, almost 100GB on-board DDR3 memory is needed. This huge memory is not
needed by using the hash-join or presorted tables combined with the merge-join. This
means that with our current system, we are able to process the query at all database
scales, even the 100TB, if the host system has the corresponding storage. The differ-
ent processing possibilities of the query can be analyzed before the processing, and an
optimizer can choose the configuration with the smallest processing time. In this case,
this would be the merge-join if the presorted tables are available and hash-join if not
combined with early or late materialization.

   ACM Transactions on Reconfigurable Technology and Systems, Vol. 9, No. 4, Article 25, Publication date: August 2016.
FPGA-Based Dynamically Reconfigurable SQL Query Processing                                                      25:23

10. CONCLUSIONS
In this article, we presented concepts and implementations for on-the-fly hardware ac-
celeration for almost all important operators appearing in SQL queries. Using partial
dynamic reconfiguration, query-specific data paths are composed on the fly. An incom-
ing SQL query is analyzed and divided into single operators and modules are subse-
quently concatenated to a data path and loaded on the FPGA. A library of partially
reconfigurable modules of SQL operators has been implemented including support for
new, important, and time-consuming operators such as joins and sorting. Different pro-
cessing strategies, like row-wise or column-wise processing, have been analyzed and
special column-wise processing modules have been introduced.
   Next, a mathematical throughput analysis was presented for performance analysis
of a query plan based on the provided query module library. Using this calculus, we
are able to analyze the data throughput for all possible generated data paths. This
is an important step to give a database management system the possibility to decide
which (sub)query is worth accelerating with hardware and which is not. Finally, the
throughput values of the analysis were compared with real measured values and a
comparison to an x86-based software system was given.
   Moreover, we proposed a PCIe-based prototype as a server extension card and SoC
prototypes based on the Xilinx Zynq platform. The processing time of these prototypes
was compared with an x86-based server and the partial reconfiguration overhead was
shown. Finally, for a given query, different processing strategies were compared on
different table sizes.

ment GmbH, for his contributions to this work.
